## 1. Sonnet vs. Haiku, resolution knee

`python scripts/m3_eval.py matrix` — 4 fixtures × {512, 768, 1092, 1568, native px long edge} ×
2 models (native tested Sonnet-only, on `neese_degraded` and `veteran_clean`).

### CER averaged across all 4 fixtures, by long edge

| Long edge | Sonnet 5 CER | Haiku 4.5 CER |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 512px | 0.000 | 0.0115 (1.15%) |
| 768px | 0.000 | 0.0013 (0.13%) |
| 1092px | 0.000 | 0.000 |
| 1568px | 0.000 | 0.0003 (~0%) |
| native | 0.000 (Sonnet only) | — |

Sonnet is CER=0.000 at every resolution tested, on every fixture, including the phone-photo and
degraded variants — it is effectively resolution-insensitive over this range on these fixtures.
Haiku has a real knee: usable but imperfect at 512px (worst case 2.1% CER on `neese_degraded`,
1.9% on `neese_phone`), a small residual at 768px (worst case 0.3%), and reaches full parity
with Sonnet (0.000 CER on every fixture) at **1092px long edge**.

### Cost per call, averaged across the 4 fixtures, by long edge

| Long edge | Sonnet 5 (intro) | Sonnet 5 (post-8/31) | Haiku 4.5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 512px | $0.0083 | $0.0124 | $0.0031 |
| 768px | $0.0090 | $0.0135 | $0.0035 |
| 1092px | $0.0102 | $0.0153 | $0.0041 |
| 1568px | $0.0106 | $0.0159 | $0.0042 |

**Haiku at its parity resolution (1092px, $0.0041) is cheaper than Sonnet at Sonnet's own
cheapest working resolution (512px, $0.0083 intro / $0.0124 post-8/31)** — roughly 2–3× cheaper
for equal (zero) measured CER on this fixture set.

### Decision — model default

Default to **Haiku 4.5 at long_edge ≥ 1092px** for transcription. Keep Sonnet as the retry tier
for low-confidence transcriptions (per the design doc's quality/cost lever, §5) rather than
promoting Haiku to a hard-only default — these fixtures are synthetic and only moderately
degraded; real century-old microfilm (open question 6) may widen the gap. The tier logic itself
is M3.4 scope; this measurement just confirms the floor is viable per open question 2.

### Decision — resolution policy

Normalize transcription input to **1568px long edge**, not the bare 1092px knee. The cost step
from 1092→1568 is small (~$0.0006–0.0008/call at either model) and buys margin for real newsprint
that's harder than these fixtures; native/full resolution showed no additional accuracy gain on
either fixture tested (`neese_degraded`, `veteran_clean`) so it isn't worth the extra tokens.
Segmentation-probe resizing (already ≤1568px per the design doc) is unaffected.

## 2. Segmentation-region accuracy

`python scripts/m3_eval.py segment` — synthetic 3-obituary page (`page_3obits.png`, ground-truth
bboxes in `page_3obits.json`), one segmentation-probe call per model, then per obituary: (a)
transcribe the model's predicted-bbox crop (3% margin) vs. (b) transcribe the full page with a
name-targeted prompt.

| Model | Found | IoU (per obit) | Probe cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sonnet 5 | 3/3 | 0.775 / 0.884 / 0.880 | $0.0086 |
| Haiku 4.5 | 3/3 | 0.724 / 0.817 / 0.753 | $0.0035 |

Both models found all 3 obituaries and rejected the filler ad. Downstream transcription CER was
0.000 for every crop and name-targeted call except one (Haiku, name-targeted, `Ada Mae (Yoder)
Miller`: 0.023). Crop-based transcription cost less than full-page name-targeted in every case
(smaller image → fewer input tokens), e.g. Sonnet/Neese: crop $0.0101 vs. name-targeted $0.0119.

### Decision

Confirms the design doc's planned M3.3 handoff: **segmentation probe → cropped-region
transcription**, not full-page name-targeted transcription. Crop-then-transcribe matches or
beats name-targeted accuracy at lower cost. Either model's probe IoU (0.72–0.88) is generous
enough for the "advisory regions + generous margin" design already specified in §4 — no bbox
tightening logic needed before M3.3.

---

## 3. PDF-input decision

`python scripts/m3_eval.py pdf` — 2-page PDF (`neese_clean` + `veteran_clean`, each resized to
1568px long edge, `application/pdf` document block) vs. the same content as two separate
per-page image calls (already measured in §1's 1568px row).

| Model | PDF CER (both pages) | PDF cost (2 pages) | Sum of 2 separate 1568px image calls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sonnet 5 | 0.000 / 0.000 | $0.0193 | $0.0094 + $0.0136 = $0.0230 |
| Haiku 4.5 | 0.000 / 0.000 | $0.0088 | $0.0038 + $0.0050 = $0.0088 |

Native PDF input transcribed both pages correctly for both models, at equal (Haiku) or ~16%
lower (Sonnet) cost than two separate image calls, and in one round trip instead of two.

### Decision

This only tested the trivial case (one clean obituary per page, no segmentation needed). The
general case — multi-obituary pages, cropping to a predicted region — requires per-page control
that native PDF input doesn't offer as cleanly. **Keep per-page image conversion as the default
ingest path** (design doc principle 1 / §3), matching what M3.1's `ingest.py` already plans.
Native PDF input is a plausible fast-path optimization for batches that are already known to be
one-clean-obituary-per-page (an M3.4 batch-workflow question, e.g. if Matthew Johnson's team
delivers pre-segmented PDFs) — revisit there, not before.

---

## 4. Cost table — transcription only, recommended defaults

Per obituary, Haiku 4.5 @ 1568px long edge (the recommended default): **$0.0038–0.0050**,
measured directly (§1, 1568px column). This replaces the design doc's §9.2 rough estimate for
the *transcription* leg specifically; the existing Haiku *extraction* leg (text→JSON, unchanged
from Milestone 1) wasn't remeasured this session — total per-obituary pipeline cost is the sum of
this transcription figure plus that unchanged extraction cost.

---

## 5. What this eval does not answer

- **Open question 6 (pre-1930 newsprint):** unresolved. These fixtures are synthetic degradation
  (rotation/blur/noise/JPEG artifact) on modern-rendered text, not real century-old microfilm.
  Needs real DCHS samples before trusting the Haiku-parity finding on genuinely old material.
- **Open question 3 (handwritten material):** out of scope, as designed.
- Segmentation was tested on one synthetic 3-obit layout; page layouts vary more in the wild.
